text.p: British retailer Liberty Plc posted first-half profits on Friday which demonstrate that it will continue to deliver positive results on the promises it made in its restructuring plans, chairman Denis Cassidy said.
"We have done precisely what we said we would do and have given a clear indication that the rest of the year will give more of what we promised," Cassidy told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Liberty's stock was marked up 15 pence to 435p following the release of first-half results.

Cassidy said the market was reacting to the fact that company was clearing up its business and clearing up its loss-making activities. Moreover, the results for the first half ended July 27 showed only the early effects of the restructuring programme.

"The thing to bear in mind in this first half is the figures from the 27th of July include only two months of the clearing up," Cassidy said. "Virtually the whole programme will be completed by the end of the trading year, certainly within the first quarter of 1997," he added.
Liberty said the restructuring provisions it established will be adequate for the entire programme.
As of July 27, Liberty had used six million stg of the total 18 million stg provision, Cassidy said.
Liberty has closed all 20 of its provincial UK stores already, as well as closing its Oxford Collection and Muji store in Glasgow.
Managing director Ian Thomson said results will continue to improve as the new management team is able to implement its merchandising strategy. The new management team took over in April.
"You'll appreciate in the retail business when you arrive in April, you're looking at merchandise that's been bought for the summer season and largely for the winter," Thomson said.

"The management we've put in place is working on Spring/Summer 1997," he said. "I think we can see some reasonable signs of improvement in Christmas," he added. "But we would be looking at improvements for 1997."

Liberty is investigating ways to expand its sales space at its flagship Regent Street store in London and in November will open a new men's clothing department in the basement using 12,000 square feet of additional space that it is turning into selling area.

Liberty, which has always been low key in promoting itself, is planning on taking a stronger message to the public, including an advertising campaign. Thomson declined to provide details of the planned campaign.

In addition, the company is continuing to build on its airport shops. It now has four shops at London's Heathrow airport, which Cassidy said play a key role in promoting the Liberty brand to consumers and acting as a bridge to carry it outside the UK.
